An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset $P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*), satisfying: - **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds: $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$. - **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.
For every $a \in F$ with $a \neq 0$ we have $a^2 > 0$, where $a^2 = a \cdot a$. In particular, every nonzero square is positive.
Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$: $$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$ More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

Let $\varepsilon_j,\mu_j>0$ be real for $j=1,2$, put $Z_j:=\sqrt{\mu_j/\varepsilon_j}$ for the nonnegative square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]], and let $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$ with $E_i\ne0$ satisfy the two linear equations $$E_i+E_r=E_t,\qquad \frac{E_i-E_r}{Z_1}=\frac{E_t}{Z_2}.$$ Then $$\frac{E_r}{E_i}=\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_2+Z_1},\qquad \frac{E_t}{E_i}=\frac{2Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2},$$ and the real numbers $R:=\bigl\lvert E_r/E_i\bigr\rvert^2$ and $T:=\bigl(Z_1/Z_2\bigr)\bigl\lvert E_t/E_i\bigr\rvert^2$ satisfy $$R+T=1 .$$

derivations.claim: [Solution of the linear system] Substituting the first equation $E_r=E_t-E_i$ into the second gives $Y_1(2E_i-E_t)=Y_2E_t$, that is $2Y_1E_i=(Y_1+Y_2)E_t$ after expanding and collecting terms by the field arithmetic of [F1]. Since $Y_1+Y_2\ne0$ is invertible in the field $\mathbb C$ by [F1], $E_t=2Y_1E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)$, and then $E_r=E_t-E_i=\bigl(2Y_1-(Y_1+Y_2)\bigr)E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)=(Y_1-Y_2)E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)$, again by [F1].

[Consequences of the solution] If $E_i\ne0$, dividing the two identities of step 1.1 by $E_i$ gives $r=E_r/E_i=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=E_t/E_i=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$. If $E_i=0$, the identities of step 1.1 give $E_t=0$ and $E_r=0$, so no field ratio exists; the algebraic expressions $r=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$ remain defined because $Y_1+Y_2\ne0$, and they agree with the field ratios whenever the latter exist. This proves (a) and the convention stated before (b).

[Modular expansions] For any $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $|z\pm w|^2=(z\pm w)(\overline z\pm\overline w)=|z|^2\pm(z\overline w+\overline z w)+|w|^2$, and $z\overline w+\overline z w=2\operatorname{Re}(z\overline w)$ by [F2]; hence for real $Y_1$ and arbitrary $Y_2$, $|Y_1\pm Y_2|^2=Y_1^2\pm2Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2+|Y_2|^2$, and subtraction gives $|Y_1+Y_2|^2-|Y_1-Y_2|^2=4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2$. Moreover $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$ and $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$: indeed $|zw|=|z||w|$ and $|z|^2=z\overline z$ by [F2] applied to the quotients of step 2.1 give $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}$ and $|t|^2=|2Y_1|^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}=4Y_1^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}$ because $(2Y_1)\overline{(2Y_1)}=4Y_1^2$ for real $Y_1$, and the denominator is nonzero since $Y_1+Y_2\ne0$.

[The flux identity] Assume $Y_1>0$ real. By [F2] and [F3], $|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$, so $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$, and the identity of step 3.1 gives $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2=1-4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$; adding $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$ cancels the correction and yields $|r|^2+(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$, the displayed identity and explicit formulas of (b).

[Sign analysis] Still with $Y_1>0$ real: since $|t|^2>0$ by step 4.1, the second summand $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2$ has the sign of $\operatorname{Re}Y_2$ by [F3], so it is nonnegative if and only if $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\ge0$. If $\operatorname{Re}Y_2<0$, then $|r|^2=1-4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>1$, and since $|r|\ge0$ and $1\ge0$, [F4] gives $|r|>1$; in that case the identity of step 4.1 has a negative transmitted term and carries no energy-conservation reading, while $|r|>1$ alone is consistent with an active transmitted model.

[Purely imaginary admittance] Assume $Y_1>0$ real and $Y_2=i\beta$ with $\beta\in\mathbb R$. Then $\overline{Y_1+Y_2}=Y_1-i\beta=Y_1-Y_2$ by [F2], so $|Y_1-Y_2|=|\overline{Y_1+Y_2}|=|Y_1+Y_2|$ by [F2] and step 3.1 gives $|r|=1$; the identity of step 4.1 then gives $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\,|t|^2=0$ (multiplying the identity by $Y_1>0$ and using $|r|^2=1$), while $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2=4Y_1^2/(Y_1^2+\beta^2)=4Y_1^2/(Y_1^2+|Y_2|^2)>0$ by [F2] and [F3]; hence $r\ne0$ because $|r|=1$ and $t\ne0$ because $|t|>0$ by the definiteness of the modulus in [F2]. This proves (c); no division by $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=0$ is performed, and the case $Y_2=0$ is included with $\beta=0$.

[Real-positive specialisation] Assume $Y_1,Y_2>0$ real. Then $Y_1-Y_2$ is real and $Y_1+Y_2>0$ is real and nonzero, so $r,t$ of step 2.1 are real by [F1], and step 4.1 gives $|r|^2+(Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$ because $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=Y_2$. Substituting $Y_j=1/Z_j$ with $Z_j>0$ real, $Y_j$ is invertible and $1/Z_1\pm1/Z_2=(Z_2\pm Z_1)/(Z_1Z_2)$ by [F1], so $r=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_1+Z_2)$ and $t=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$ by cancellation of the nonzero factor $Z_1Z_2$; moreover $Y_2/Y_1=Z_1/Z_2$ by [F1], so the balance is $R+T=1$ for $R=|r|^2$ and $T=(Z_1/Z_2)|t|^2$. These are exactly the solution formulas and the balance of [F5], so clause (d) is in agreement with [[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]].

The period-averaged normal fluxes: for (s), the flux of [F1] is $\langle S_j\rangle=|e_j|^2k_j/(2\mu_j\omega)$ with $|e_j|^2=|E^{(s)}_j|^2$ and $k_j\cdot n=k_{j3}$, so the normal fluxes are $k_{j3}|E^{(s)}_j|^2/(2\mu_j\omega)$, i.e. $Y^s_1|E^{(s)}_i|^2/2$, $-Y^s_1|E^{(s)}_r|^2/2$, $Y^s_2|E^{(s)}_t|^2/2$; for (p) the same $\langle S_j\cdot n\rangle=|e_j|^2k_{j3}/(2\mu_j\omega)$ equals $Y^p_j\,|E^{(p)}_j|^2/2$ up to the reflected sign, because $|e_j|^2=\mu_j|H_j|^2/\varepsilon_j$ and $|E^{(p)}_j|=|k_{j3}||H_j|/(\varepsilon_j\omega)$ give $|e_j|^2k_{j3}/(2\mu_j\omega)=k_{j3}|H_j|^2/(2\varepsilon_j\omega)$ for the incident and transmitted signs, while the reflected signed component $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$ produces the minus sign, as in the Statement. With $R_\chi=|r_\chi|^2=|E^\chi_r|^2/|E^\chi_i|^2$ and $T_\chi=(Y^\chi_2/Y^\chi_1)|t_\chi|^2=Y^\chi_2|E^\chi_t|^2/(Y^\chi_1|E^\chi_i|^2)$, the budget $R_\chi+T_\chi=1$ is [F3](b) applied with the real positive $Y^\chi_1,Y^\chi_2$.

[Total internal reflection, part (d)] Let $|\kappa|>K_2$; then $K_2<K_1$, so $n_2<n_1$, and $k_{t3}=i\beta$ with $\beta=\sqrt{|\kappa|^2-K_2^2}>0$ by [F6]. Hence $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)=i\beta/(\mu_2\omega)$ and $Y^p_2=\varepsilon_2\omega/(i\beta)=-i\varepsilon_2\omega/\beta$ are purely imaginary by [F7], while $Y^\chi_1>0$ is real; the admittance lemma [F3](c) gives $|r_s|=|r_p|=1$ and $|t_\chi|^2=4(Y^\chi_1)^2/((Y^\chi_1)^2+|Y^\chi_2|^2)>0$, so $t_\chi\ne0$. The transmitted wave is the evanescent branch of [F1] with $n'=n$, $\kappa_0=\kappa$ and $k_t\cdot k_t=K_2^2=\varepsilon_2\mu_2\omega^2$: the field factorizes with the decay factor $e^{-\beta x_3}$, its period-averaged normal flux vanishes identically, and its tangential averaged flux is strictly positive; since $|r_\chi|=1$, the reflected normal averaged flux equals minus the incident normal averaged flux, i.e. the reflected wave carries the whole incident normal averaged flux.

[Brewster condition, part (c)] In each finite-admittance branch the formula of step 3.1 gives $r_\chi=0$ exactly when the numerator $Y^\chi_1-Y^\chi_2$ vanishes, i.e. $Y^\chi_1=Y^\chi_2$. Assume now $\mu_1=\mu_2=:\mu$ and $|\kappa|<K_2$, so that the (p) admittances are real positive. The condition $Y^p_1=Y^p_2$ reads $\varepsilon_1/k_{13}=\varepsilon_2/k_{t3}$; substituting $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$ and $k_{j3}=(\omega n_j/c)\cos\theta_j$ (from $k_{13}=K_1\cos\theta_i=(\omega n_1/c)\cos\theta_i$ and $k_{t3}=K_2\cos\theta_t=(\omega n_2/c)\cos\theta_t$) gives $n_1\cos\theta_t=n_2\cos\theta_i$. Together with Snell's law $n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$ of step 4.1, squaring both and eliminating $\sin^2\theta_t$ gives $(n_1^2-n_2^2)\bigl[n_2^2-(n_1^2+n_2^2)\sin^2\theta_i\bigr]=0$: indeed $n_1^2(1-\sin^2\theta_t)=n_2^2\cos^2\theta_i$ and $\sin\theta_t=(n_1/n_2)\sin\theta_i$ yield $n_1^2n_2^2-n_1^4\sin^2\theta_i=n_2^4-n_2^4\sin^2\theta_i$, i.e. $n_2^2(n_1^2-n_2^2)=(n_1^2-n_2^2)(n_1^2+n_2^2)\sin^2\theta_i$. If $n_1\ne n_2$, division by the nonzero first factor gives $\sin^2\theta_i=n_2^2/(n_1^2+n_2^2)$; since $0<\theta_i<\pi/2$ and sine is strictly increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$ with $\sin 0=0$ by [F8], this determines the unique admissible angle $\theta_B:=\arcsin\bigl(n_2/\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}\bigr)\in(0,\pi/2)$, This angle is admissible: with $D:=\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}$, its tangential wavenumber is $K_1n_2/D<K_2$ because $n_1/D<1$. Snell's law therefore gives $\sin\theta_t=n_1/D$ and, by positivity of both cosines and the Pythagorean identity, $\cos\theta_i=n_1/D$, $\cos\theta_t=n_2/D$. Thus $n_1\cos\theta_t=n_2\cos\theta_i$, establishing $Y_1^p=Y_2^p$ and $r_p=0$; this proves sufficiency as well as uniqueness. At this angle $\cos\theta_B>0$: cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ by [F8], so $0<\theta_B<\pi/2$ gives $\cos\theta_B>\cos(\pi/2)=0$. The Pythagorean identity of [F8] then gives $\cos\theta_B=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta_B}=n_1/\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}$, so $\tan\theta_B=\sin\theta_B/\cos\theta_B=n_2/n_1$ by the definition of tangent in [F8]; no other admissible angle has this tangent, because tangent is strictly increasing on $(0,\pi/2)$ by [F8]. Also $r_s\ne0$ at $\theta_B$, because $Y^s_1=Y^s_2$ would give $k_{13}=k_{t3}$ (the $\mu$ factors being equal), hence $K_1^2=|\kappa|^2+k_{13}^2=|\kappa|^2+k_{t3}^2=K_2^2$ and $n_1=n_2$, contrary to hypothesis. If instead $n_1=n_2$ and $\mu_1=\mu_2$ then $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$ and the two media are identical: $k_{13}=k_{t3}$ and $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$ give $Y^\chi_1=Y^\chi_2$, so $r_s=r_p=0$ and $t_s=t_p=1$ at every admissible angle (where the (p) formula applies), with no distinguished Brewster angle.

Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], in its isotropic scalar case: the material is at rest in the laboratory frame, $D,H$ are defined by [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]](d), and the constitutive relations of [[post-em-material-closure]](b) hold with constant scalars $\varepsilon>0$ (F$\,$m$^{-1}$), $\mu>0$ (H$\,$m$^{-1}$) and $\sigma\ge0$ (S$\,$m$^{-1}$), so that $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ and the free current is $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Write $c>0$ for the exact vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and let $\omega>0$ (s$^{-1}$) be an angular frequency. Define:

**(a) [Lossless parameters]** with $\sqrt{\cdot}$ the nonnegative square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]],
$$v:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}\quad(\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}),\qquad Z:=\Bigl(\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^{1/2}\quad(\Omega),\qquad n:=\frac{c}{v}=c(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}\quad(\text{dimensionless}),\qquad k(\omega):=\frac{\omega}{v};$$
$v$ is the phase speed, $Z$ the wave impedance, $n$ the refractive index relative to vacuum and $k(\omega)$ the real wavenumber of the lossless case.

**(b) [Complex propagation constant]** put $a:=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}>0$, $b:=\mu\sigma\omega\ge0$, $r:=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ and
$$p(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r+a}{2}},\qquad q(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r-a}{2}},\qquad \kappa(\omega):=p(\omega)+i\,q(\omega).$$
Then $\kappa(\omega)$ is the unique $k\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}k\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}k\ge0$ and $k^{2}=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega=a+ib$; in the lossless case $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $q=0$ and $\kappa(\omega)=k(\omega)=p(\omega)$ real. (The explicit formula is the one of [[thm-every-complex-number-has-a-square-root]]; the verification $p^{2}-q^{2}=a$, $2pq=b$ and the uniqueness of the root with $\operatorname{Re}k\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}k\ge0$ are verified in the well-definedness paragraph below.)

**(c) [Skin depth]** call $\delta(\omega):=1/q(\omega)$ (m) the skin depth if $\sigma>0$, and set $\delta(\omega):=+\infty$ if $\sigma=0$: for $\kappa(\omega)=p+iq$ and $x_3\in\mathbb R$ the modulus of $e^{i(\kappa x_3-\omega t)}$ equals $e^{-q x_3}$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]), so $\delta$ is the distance in which that modulus decays by the factor $1/e$ in the direction of increasing $x_3$; for $\sigma=0$ there is no attenuation and $\delta$ is infinite rather than a division by zero.

**(d) [Status and scope]** This item fixes objects, units, branch conventions and terminology only. It asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation for a solution, no attenuation of any concrete field and no material validity. The parameters are declared for the isotropic scalar constant-coefficient branch at rest in the laboratory frame; for $\varepsilon\mu<c^{-2}$ the branch is, by [[post-em-material-closure]](b), a declared finite-band effective phase-response model with no universal front-speed claim. An exact broadband interpretation must be separately adopted and requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$; that inequality alone does not adopt a broadband interpretation or establish material validity, and a finite-band interpretation remains possible when it holds. ### Well-definedness and conventions

The material assumptions, the rest-frame clause, the isotropic scalar case and the finite-band caveat are those of [[post-em-material-closure]](a)-(b) read with [[def-em-polarization-magnetization|the polarization and magnetization definitions]]; the unit system and the exact constant $c$ are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; the laboratory chart is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

The only content beyond notation is the well-definedness of $\kappa(\omega)$ in (b). With $a>0$, $b\ge0$ and $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ one has $r+a>0$ and $(r-a)(r+a)=b^2\ge0$, so $r-a\ge0$ and both defining radicands are nonnegative. If $b>0$, the same identity gives $r-a>0$, hence $q>0$; if $b=0$, uniqueness of nonnegative roots gives $r=a$ and $q=0$. Also $p>0$ because $r+a>0$. In the lossless case $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $r=a$, $q=0$, $p=\sqrt a=\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}=k(\omega)$ by [[thm-of-square-roots]].
